extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors, patent litigators, patent examiners, and patent practitioners working on U.S. §101 Alice/Mayo issues (software, computer-implemented, and technical patents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and case-based criteria for evaluating whether patent claims satisfy 35 U.S.C. §101 under the Alice/Mayo two-step framework (including the USPTO/PTAB Revised Step 2A prongs and Step 2B). Focuses on software/computer-implemented, data-processing, and other technical inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed to an abstract idea (Alice Step 1 / Prong One)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea (e.g., collecting, analyzing, manipulating, displaying information; mental processes; fundamental economic practices; mathematical concepts; certain methods of organizing human activity; communications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the document: 'collecting, displaying, and analyzing information'; 'the broad concept of communicating information wirelessly, without more, is an abstract idea'; claims that capture only information or high-level concepts are often found to be directed to abstract ideas. PTAB/Fed. Cir. decisions classify many data-processing and business-practice claims under this rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept / Alice Step 2 (or Revised Step 2A Prong Two / Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim recites an 'inventive concept' that transforms the abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter — i.e., limitations that are significantly more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and cases: an inventive concept can be 'found in the non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of known, conventional pieces' (Berkheimer); factual allegations/declarations can show claims are not routine/conventional (Aatrix). If the only additional features are generic computer components or routine data-handling, no inventive concept exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to computer or other technology (Step 1 non-abstract)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are 'directed to an improvement in computer functionality' or solve a technological problem (improve speed, accuracy, usability, memory function, security, etc.) may not be abstract at Alice Step 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fed. Cir. precedents cited: Enfish (self-referential database), DDR Holdings, Trading Technologies (GUI addressing speed/accuracy/usability), Koninklijke (error checking in data transmission), and cases finding enhanced memory systems or network security improvements. The claim must show specifics of the technological improvement, not merely add conventional components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of claim limitations vs. high-level results
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that provide specific steps/structure for achieving a result (a 'way to achieve it') rather than claiming only a desired result are more likely to be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document: 'Claims directed to an improvement ... have specificity required to transform a claim from one claiming only a result to one claiming a way to achieve it.' Lack of detail about how high-level functions are done leads to ineligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recitation of only generic computer components is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply reciting generic computer hardware (processor, storage device, server, receiver, standard components) does not make an abstract idea patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple decisions: standard components 'are not sufficient to transform abstract claims into patent-eligible subject matter.' Examiners and courts frequently reject claims where the only added elements are routine computer implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims performable by a human mind (mental processes) are abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: If claims, when construed broadly, can be performed in the human mind (collecting, comparing, making determinations), they fall into the mental-process category of abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: coupon fraud detection by comparing data, collecting/comparing information, methods of organizing human activity. PTAB and courts have found such claims abstract when they essentially describe observation, evaluation, and judgment steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical algorithms and mathematical concepts are abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite mathematical algorithms, calculations, mapping coordinates, or pure mathematical concepts are treated as abstract ideas unless integrated into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document: 'Claims recite mathematical concepts and thus abstract ideas under Prong One of the Guidance.' 'Merely calling for a mathematical algorithm to be performed more efficiently ... is not patent eligible.' Use of mathematical output in a concrete application (e.g., controlling a machine, producing an image used to drill) can render eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural laws / natural principles usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims 'directed to the utilization of a natural law' (e.g., Hooke's law, methods of detecting body temperature based on natural principles) implicate Mayo-type exclusion if the claim simply applies the law without more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim employs a natural law, courts ask whether the claim integrates that law into an inventive concept or merely uses it in a conventional way. Non-conventional measurement/technique supported by the specification may favor eligibility (Kukkonen example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application / integration into a machine or technical environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the alleged abstract idea is integrated into a practical application (Prong Two of Revised Step 2A), such as specific software steps, particular machine implementation, or hardware that produces a technological result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If integration into a practical application is found, the analysis often stops (Step 2A prong two) and later steps may be unnecessary. Examples: UI layering that provides evaluation via on-screen cursor (PTAB polling GUI); integration of algorithms into catheter navigation machine; producing an image of a subsurface region.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-conventional, non-generic arrangement of known elements
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventive concept can arise from arranging known, conventional elements in a non-conventional and non-generic way that achieves a technological improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Berkheimer language: a non-conventional and non-generic arrangement can confer patent eligibility. Courts look to specification support and factual evidence to determine whether arrangement is conventional or not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption analysis — limit claim scope to avoid broad preemption
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether claim limitations and specific structure prevent broad preemption of all ways to achieve the abstract idea is relevant; claims that would preempt all approaches are more likely to be ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McRO noted that specific structure of claimed rules would prevent broad preemption; courts consider whether limitations meaningfully restrict use of the abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardware transformation / machine-or-transformation considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardware elements that transform data into a concrete result or otherwise effect a machine-or-transformation can weigh in favor of eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document references 'hardware elements that transform data into a concrete result.' However, mere invocation of a machine is not always sufficient—courts assess whether the machine imposes meaningful limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improving user interface or presenting information in a specific structured way
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that require a 'particular manner of summarizing and presenting information' or a specific, structured GUI that solves identified problems can be non-abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DDR Holdings and Trading Technologies examples: requirements for a specific structured GUI paired with prescribed functionality that resolves problems in prior art support Step 1 eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional activity in a new environment is not 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying an old practice (e.g., sending a notification) in a new technological environment without more does not make a claim patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Sending a notification is not significantly more. An old practice in a new environment.' Courts treat mere field-of-use or environment changes as insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that only provide information or additional data are typically ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims whose main contribution is providing information or adding additional data to a prior art user interface generally do not pass §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document: claims that 'only provide the information were not eligible' and adding additional data to a prior art UI did not supply an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and factual allegations may prevent dismissal on §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Plausible factual allegations and supporting evidence (e.g., declarations, specification details) that an asserted claim contains inventive concepts can preclude dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6) on §101 grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aatrix: court held district court improperly dismissed where plaintiff's factual allegations could show inventive concept; examiners and courts should provide reasoning/evidence when finding components 'routine' or 'well-understood.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims vs. independent claims — factual questions may arise
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent claims that add specific limitations may raise factual disputes about whether they contain limitations directed to an arguable inventive concept even when independent claims are found ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Berkheimer/Berkheimer-type fact questions: the Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment on dependent claims where specification suggested dependent claims might contain unconventional inventive concepts (e.g., reducing redundancy in object storage).
